prompt: According to the section, the preferred phase of a substance under a given set of conditions is a balance between which two things?

choices.text: The energy of the particles and the intermolecular forces between them
The mass of the sample and the volume of its container
choices.why: A bigger or smaller sample doesn't change its phase. Phase depends on how strongly the particles attract each other compared with how much energy they have.

choices.text: The number of atoms in each molecule and the strength of the covalent bonds inside it
choices.why: Covalent bonds hold atoms together within a molecule. Phase depends on the forces between separate particles, weighed against the particles' energy.

choices.text: The color of the substance and its density
choices.why: Color and density are properties of a phase, not what decides it. The balance is between particle energy and intermolecular forces.

explanation: If the forces between particles are strong enough compared with the particles' energy, the substance is a liquid or, if stronger, a solid. If the forces are weak and there is enough energy, the particles separate and the substance is a gas.

prompt: Which variable mostly determines the energy of the particles in a substance, and so is the main variable that decides which phase is stable?

choices.text: Temperature
Molar mass
choices.why: Molar mass affects how strong the intermolecular forces are, but it is fixed for a substance. The particles' energy is mostly set by temperature.

choices.text: The size of the container
choices.why: Moving a sample to a bigger container doesn't give its particles more energy. Temperature does.

choices.text: The number of particles in the sample
choices.why: More particles means more substance, not more energy per particle. The energy of each particle is mostly set by temperature.

explanation: The energy of the particles is mostly determined by temperature, so temperature is the main variable that determines which phase is stable at any given point.

prompt: The forces between the particles of a substance are very strong compared with the energy the particles have. Which phase is the substance most likely in?

choices.text: Solid
Liquid
choices.why: Forces strong enough to hold particles together give a liquid; even stronger forces, which hold the particles in place, give a solid.

choices.text: Gas
choices.why: A gas forms when the forces are weak and the particles have enough energy to separate. Very strong forces keep the particles together.

choices.text: It can't be predicted, because phase doesn't depend on intermolecular forces
choices.why: Phase depends directly on intermolecular forces, weighed against the particles' energy.

explanation: If the forces between particles are strong enough, the substance is a liquid or, if stronger, a solid. Weak forces with enough energy give a gas.

prompt: Which intermolecular force is present in all substances that have electrons?

choices.text: The dispersion force
Dipole-dipole interactions
choices.why: Dipole-dipole interactions need molecules with a permanent dipole, so only polar substances have them.

choices.text: Hydrogen bonding
choices.why: Hydrogen bonding needs an H atom bonded to an N, O, or F atom, so most substances don't have it.

choices.text: The attraction between oppositely charged ions
choices.why: That attraction holds ionic compounds together, but most substances are not made of ions. The force every substance has is the dispersion force.

explanation: The dispersion force (London dispersion force) comes from the movement of electrons, so every substance with electrons experiences it, polar or not.

prompt: What causes the dispersion force between molecules?

choices.text: At any instant an electron's position makes one part of a molecule slightly negative and the rest slightly positive, and these fleeting imbalances let molecules attract each other.
The permanent partial charges on the ends of polar molecules attract each other.
choices.why: That describes dipole-dipole interactions. Dispersion forces come from temporary imbalances that shift as electrons move, so even nonpolar molecules have them.

choices.text: An H atom bonded to N, O, or F in one molecule attracts another molecule.
choices.why: That describes hydrogen bonding. Dispersion forces need only electrons.

choices.text: Electrons are transferred from one molecule to another, forming ions that attract.
choices.why: No electrons are transferred. The imbalance is inside each molecule and lasts only an instant.

explanation: The instantaneous position of an electron temporarily makes one point of a molecule negative and the rest positive. A moment later the electron is elsewhere, but these fleeting imbalances of charge let molecules interact.

prompt: The halogens F2, Cl2, Br2, and I2 are all nonpolar, so dispersion forces are the only intermolecular forces between their molecules. Which has the strongest dispersion forces?

choices.text: I2
F2
choices.why: F2 has the fewest electrons (18) of the four, so its dispersion forces are the weakest; that's why it is a gas at room temperature.

choices.text: Cl2
choices.why: Cl2 has 34 electrons, more than F2 but fewer than Br2 and I2. More electrons means stronger dispersion forces.

choices.text: All four are the same, because all four are nonpolar
choices.why: Being nonpolar means they have only dispersion forces, but the strength of those forces grows with the number of electrons.

explanation: The greater the number of electrons in a species, the stronger the dispersion force. I2 has the most electrons (106), so its dispersion forces are strongest, which is why I2 is a solid at room temperature while F2 and Cl2 are gases.

prompt: The strength of the dispersion force grows with the number of electrons in a molecule. How many electrons does one Cl2 molecule have? (Cl has atomic number 17.)
explanation: Each Cl atom has 17 electrons (its atomic number), so Cl2 has 2 × 17 = 34 electrons.

prompt: At the same temperature, smaller molecules are often gases while larger molecules are liquids or solids. Which statement helps explain this?

choices.text: Larger molecules have more electrons, so their dispersion forces are stronger.
Larger molecules always have hydrogen bonding, and smaller molecules never do.
choices.why: Hydrogen bonding depends on an H atom bonded to N, O, or F, not on size. Water is small and has it; large hydrocarbons are big and don't.

choices.text: The covalent bonds inside smaller molecules are weaker, so the molecules fall apart into gases.
choices.why: A substance becomes a gas when its molecules separate from each other, not when the molecules themselves break apart.

choices.text: Larger molecules are always polar, and smaller molecules are always nonpolar.
choices.why: Size doesn't decide polarity; H2O is small and polar, and large hydrocarbons are nonpolar.

explanation: The more electrons a species has, the stronger its dispersion force. This partially explains why smaller molecules are gases and larger molecules are liquids and solids at the same temperature. (Mass is a factor as well.)

prompt: Which molecules experience dipole-dipole interactions?

choices.text: Molecules with a permanent dipole moment, whose oppositely charged ends attract each other
Every molecule, because every molecule has electrons
choices.why: Every molecule has dispersion forces. Dipole-dipole interactions need a permanent dipole, so only polar molecules have them.

choices.text: Only molecules with an H atom bonded to N, O, or F
choices.why: Those molecules have hydrogen bonding, an unusually strong kind of dipole-dipole interaction. Any polar molecule has dipole-dipole interactions.

choices.text: Only molecules made of ions
choices.why: Ions are held by the attraction of full charges. Dipole-dipole interactions are between the partial charges on the ends of polar molecules.

explanation: Molecules with a permanent dipole moment experience dipole-dipole interactions: the oppositely charged ends of polar molecules, which carry partial charges, attract each other.

prompt: CH2Cl2 (molar mass 85 g/mol) boils at 313 K, while CF4 (molar mass 88 g/mol) boils at only 145 K. Both molecules have 42 electrons. Why does CH2Cl2 boil at the much higher temperature?

choices.text: CH2Cl2 is polar, so it has dipole-dipole interactions; CF4 is nonpolar and has only dispersion forces.
CH2Cl2 has stronger dispersion forces because it has more electrons.
choices.why: Both molecules have 42 electrons, so their dispersion forces are similar. The difference is that CH2Cl2 is polar.

choices.text: CH2Cl2 has hydrogen bonding because it contains H atoms.
choices.why: Its H atoms are bonded to C, not to N, O, or F, so CH2Cl2 has no hydrogen bonding.

choices.text: CH2Cl2 is heavier, and heavier molecules boil at higher temperatures.
choices.why: CH2Cl2 is actually the lighter of the two (85 vs 88 g/mol), yet it boils higher, because it is polar.

explanation: Dipole-dipole interactions are generally stronger than dispersion forces when all other things are equal. CH2Cl2 is polar and CF4 is not, so CH2Cl2 boils at a much higher temperature even though its molar mass is lower.

prompt: CF4 is a nonpolar molecule whose only intermolecular forces are dispersion forces, so it boils at just 145 K. What is this boiling point in degrees Celsius?
Two substances have molecules with about the same number of electrons and about the same mass. One is polar and the other is nonpolar. Which statement is most likely true?

choices.text: The polar substance has the higher boiling point.
The nonpolar substance has the higher boiling point, because only nonpolar molecules have dispersion forces.
choices.why: All substances have dispersion forces. The polar substance has dispersion forces and dipole-dipole interactions, so its molecules hold together more strongly.

choices.text: They have the same boiling point, because their dispersion forces are the same.
choices.why: Their dispersion forces are similar, but the polar substance also has dipole-dipole interactions, which raise its boiling point.

choices.text: The polar substance has the lower boiling point, because the partial charges on its molecules repel each other.
choices.why: Polar molecules line up so that oppositely charged ends meet, and those ends attract. That attraction raises the boiling point.

explanation: Dipole-dipole interactions are generally stronger than dispersion forces if all other things are equal, so the polar substance needs more energy to separate its molecules and boils at a higher temperature.

prompt: Hydrogen bonding is found in molecules that have an H atom bonded to which atoms?

choices.text: N, O, or F
C, N, or O
choices.why: C–H bonds are only minimally polar, so an H bonded to C doesn't take part in hydrogen bonding. The partners are N, O, and F.

choices.text: Cl, Br, or I
choices.why: H bonded to Cl, Br, or I gives a polar molecule with dipole-dipole interactions, but not hydrogen bonding. Only N, O, and F make the bond polar enough.

choices.text: Any nonmetal
choices.why: Only H bonded to N, O, or F makes bonds polar enough for hydrogen bonding.

explanation: Hydrogen bonding is found in molecules with an H atom bonded to an N atom, an O atom, or an F atom. These covalent bonds are very polar, and the interaction between them in different molecules is strong enough to be its own category of intermolecular force.

prompt: Which statement best describes hydrogen bonding?

choices.text: An unusually strong form of dipole-dipole interaction between molecules
The covalent bond between an H atom and an O atom inside a water molecule
choices.why: That bond is inside the molecule. Hydrogen bonding is an attraction between molecules.

choices.text: The dispersion force between molecules of hydrogen gas, H2
choices.why: H2 has only dispersion forces; it has no H bonded to N, O, or F. Hydrogen bonding is a strong dipole-dipole interaction.

choices.text: An ionic bond between an H^+ ion and a negative ion
choices.why: Hydrogen bonding involves polar molecules, not ions. It is a strong attraction between very polar bonds in different molecules.

explanation: Hydrogen bonding is an unusually strong form of dipole-dipole interaction. The H–N, H–O, and H–F bonds are so polar that the attraction between them in two or more molecules forms a category of its own.

prompt: Which of these substances experiences hydrogen bonding?

choices.text: NH3
PH3
choices.why: PH3 has H atoms bonded to P, which is not N, O, or F, so it has no hydrogen bonding.

choices.text: CH3F
choices.why: CH3F contains both H and F, but its H atoms are bonded to C, not to F. Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded directly to N, O, or F.

choices.text: CH4
choices.why: CH4's H atoms are bonded to C, so it has only dispersion forces.

explanation: In NH3 each H atom is bonded directly to an N atom, so NH3 experiences hydrogen bonding.

prompt: A student says that fluoromethane, CH3F, has hydrogen bonding because its molecule contains both H atoms and an F atom. What is wrong with this reasoning?

choices.text: Hydrogen bonding needs an H atom bonded directly to N, O, or F; in CH3F the H atoms are bonded to C.
Hydrogen bonding needs an H atom bonded to Cl, not F.
choices.why: H bonded to Cl gives dipole-dipole interactions, not hydrogen bonding. F is one of the right partners; the problem is that it isn't bonded to H here.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong; any molecule containing H and F has hydrogen bonding.
choices.why: What matters is which atoms are bonded to each other. The H atoms in CH3F are bonded to C, so there is no hydrogen bonding.

choices.text: Only molecules with exactly two atoms can have hydrogen bonding.
choices.why: H2O, NH3, and many larger molecules have hydrogen bonding. The requirement is an H bonded to N, O, or F.

explanation: Hydrogen bonding is found in molecules with an H atom bonded to an N, O, or F atom. CH3F has H and F in the same molecule, but no H–F bond, so its most significant intermolecular force is dipole-dipole interaction.

prompt: How many of these substances experience hydrogen bonding: NH3, CH4, H2O2, H2S, C2H5OH (ethanol, with an O–H bond), and CH3F?
explanation: NH3 (H bonded to N), H2O2 (H bonded to O), and C2H5OH (its O–H bond) have hydrogen bonding: 3 substances. CH4 and CH3F have H bonded only to C, and H2S has H bonded to S, which is not N, O, or F.

prompt: What is the most significant intermolecular force in butane, C4H10?

choices.text: Dispersion forces
Dipole-dipole interactions
choices.why: C–H bonds are only minimally polar, so a hydrocarbon like butane is essentially nonpolar.

choices.text: Hydrogen bonding
choices.why: Butane's H atoms are bonded to C, not to N, O, or F.

choices.text: Ionic attractions
choices.why: Butane is a molecular compound made of C and H; it has no ions.

explanation: Although C–H bonds are polar, they are only minimally polar, so the most significant intermolecular force in a hydrocarbon like C4H10 is dispersion forces.

prompt: What is the most significant intermolecular force in hydrogen bromide, HBr?

choices.text: Dipole-dipole interactions
Hydrogen bonding
choices.why: HBr has an H atom, but it is bonded to Br, not to N, O, or F, so there is no hydrogen bonding.

choices.text: Dispersion forces only
choices.why: HBr does have dispersion forces, but the H–Br bond is polar, so HBr also has a permanent dipole and the stronger dipole-dipole interactions.

choices.text: Ionic attractions
choices.why: HBr is a covalent molecule. Its partial charges come from a polar bond, not from ions.

explanation: HBr has a polar H–Br bond, so the molecule has a permanent dipole. Because the H is bonded to Br rather than N, O, or F, there's no hydrogen bonding, and the most significant force is dipole-dipole interaction.

prompt: VSEPR shows that sulfur dioxide, SO2, is a bent molecule. What is its most significant intermolecular force?

choices.text: Dipole-dipole interactions
Dispersion forces only, because S and O are both nonmetals
choices.why: Bonds between two nonmetals can still be polar. The S–O bonds are polar, and in a bent molecule their dipoles don't cancel, so SO2 is polar.

choices.text: Hydrogen bonding
choices.why: SO2 has no H atoms at all, so it can't have hydrogen bonding.

choices.text: Ionic attractions
choices.why: SO2 is a covalently bonded molecule, not an ionic compound.

explanation: SO2 is bent, so the dipoles of its polar S–O bonds don't cancel and the molecule has a permanent dipole. Its most significant intermolecular force is dipole-dipole interaction.

prompt: The C=O bonds in carbon dioxide, CO2, are polar, and the molecule is linear. What is the most significant intermolecular force in CO2?

choices.text: Dispersion forces
Dipole-dipole interactions
choices.why: The bonds are polar, but in a linear molecule the two bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel, so CO2 has no permanent dipole.

choices.text: Hydrogen bonding
choices.why: CO2 has no H atoms, so it can't have hydrogen bonding.

choices.text: Ionic attractions
choices.why: CO2 is a molecular compound, not an ionic one.

explanation: In linear CO2 the two polar C=O bonds point in opposite directions, so their dipoles cancel and the molecule is nonpolar. That leaves dispersion forces as its intermolecular force.

prompt: Which substance experiences dipole-dipole interactions but not hydrogen bonding?

choices.text: CH3Cl
H2O
choices.why: H2O has H atoms bonded to O, so it has hydrogen bonding.

choices.text: CCl4
choices.why: CCl4 is tetrahedral with four identical C–Cl bonds whose dipoles cancel, so it is nonpolar and has only dispersion forces.

choices.text: NH3
choices.why: NH3 has H atoms bonded to N, so it has hydrogen bonding.

explanation: CH3Cl has one polar C–Cl bond and three C–H bonds, so its bond dipoles don't cancel and it is polar. Its H atoms are bonded to C, so it has dipole-dipole interactions but no hydrogen bonding.

prompt: Water (molar mass 18 g/mol) boils at 100°C, while hydrogen sulfide, H2S (molar mass 34 g/mol), boils at −60°C. Why does water boil at such a high temperature for a small molecule?

choices.text: Water molecules experience hydrogen bonding, and H2S molecules do not.
Water molecules are heavier than H2S molecules.
choices.why: Water is the lighter molecule (18 vs 34 g/mol). It boils higher in spite of that, because of hydrogen bonding.

choices.text: Boiling water has to break its strong O–H covalent bonds.
choices.why: Boiling separates whole molecules from each other; the O–H bonds inside each molecule stay intact.

choices.text: Water molecules have more electrons, so their dispersion forces are stronger.
choices.why: H2O has 10 electrons and H2S has 18, so H2S has the stronger dispersion forces. Hydrogen bonding is what makes water different.

explanation: H2O molecules experience hydrogen bonding, while H2S molecules do not. This strong attraction between H2O molecules takes extra energy to overcome, so water's boiling point is much higher than expected for its size.

prompt: Water boils at 373 K. Hydrogen sulfide, H2S, a similar molecule without hydrogen bonding, boils at 213 K. How many kelvins higher is water's boiling point?
explanation: 373 K − 213 K = 160 K. Hydrogen bonding between H2O molecules takes extra energy to overcome, which accounts for the much higher boiling point.

prompt: A student explains that water has a high boiling point because boiling must break the strong O–H bonds in every water molecule. What is wrong with this explanation?

choices.text: Boiling separates water molecules from each other by overcoming hydrogen bonds between them; the O–H bonds inside each molecule are not broken.
Boiling breaks the O–H bonds, but they are weak, so they don't explain the high boiling point.
choices.why: Boiling doesn't break the O–H bonds at all. Steam is still H2O; what is overcome is the attraction between molecules.

choices.text: Water's boiling point isn't high; 100°C is typical for a molecule of its size.
choices.why: It is unusually high: H2S, a similar molecule, boils at −60°C. Hydrogen bonding is the reason.

choices.text: Boiling breaks the bond between the two H atoms in a water molecule.
choices.why: The two H atoms in water are each bonded to O, not to each other, and boiling breaks no covalent bonds.

explanation: When a liquid boils, its molecules separate from each other. For water that means overcoming hydrogen bonds between molecules, which takes extra energy, while the covalent O–H bonds within each molecule stay intact.

prompt: Why is ice less dense than liquid water?

choices.text: Hydrogen bonding lines the molecules up in a way that leaves empty space between them, so the solid takes up more volume.
Freezing breaks the hydrogen bonds, so the molecules spread farther apart.
choices.why: It's the other way around: in ice, hydrogen bonding holds the molecules in a pattern that leaves extra space between them.

choices.text: Water molecules get bigger when they freeze.
choices.why: The molecules stay the same size. Their arrangement in ice leaves more empty space between them.

choices.text: Ice molecules move faster than liquid water molecules, so they push each other apart.
choices.why: Particles in a solid have less energy than in the liquid. The extra volume comes from how hydrogen bonding lines up the molecules.

explanation: When water solidifies, hydrogen bonding forces the molecules to line up in a way that creates empty space between them, increasing the volume of the solid. That's why ice is less dense than liquid water and expands when it freezes.

prompt: The section credits hydrogen bonding with several of water's unusual properties. Which is one of them?

choices.text: Its high heat capacity
Its low molar mass
choices.why: Molar mass comes from the atoms in the molecule, not from forces between molecules. Water's low molar mass makes its high boiling point all the more surprising.

choices.text: Its being made of hydrogen and oxygen
choices.why: That's water's composition, not a property caused by hydrogen bonding.

choices.text: Its O–H bonds breaking when it boils
choices.why: The O–H bonds don't break when water boils. Hydrogen bonding explains water's high boiling point, not broken bonds.

explanation: Hydrogen bonding is responsible for water's relatively high melting and boiling points, its ability as a solvent, its high heat capacity, and its expansion when it freezes.

prompt: The noble gases He, Ne, Ar, and Kr exist as single atoms, and dispersion forces are the only forces between them. Which has the highest boiling point?

choices.text: Kr
He
choices.why: He has only 2 electrons, so its dispersion forces are the weakest of the four, and it has the lowest boiling point.

choices.text: Ne
choices.why: Ne has 10 electrons, fewer than Ar and Kr, so its dispersion forces are weaker than theirs.

choices.text: They all boil at the same temperature, because they have the same kind of force
choices.why: They have the same kind of force, but its strength grows with the number of electrons.

explanation: The more electrons a species has, the stronger its dispersion force. Kr has the most electrons (36) of the four, so it takes the most energy to separate its atoms.

prompt: At low temperatures most substances are solids. Which substance is predicted to remain a liquid even at absolute zero?

choices.text: Helium
Mercury
choices.why: Mercury is a liquid at room temperature, but it freezes at −38.8°C, far above absolute zero.

choices.text: Water
choices.why: Water freezes at 0°C. Thanks to hydrogen bonding, it is solid long before absolute zero.

choices.text: Hydrogen
choices.why: Hydrogen has very weak intermolecular forces, but it still freezes, at about 14 K. Only helium is predicted to stay liquid.

explanation: At low temperatures, most substances are solids; only helium is predicted to be a liquid at absolute zero.

prompt: A solid has very weak intermolecular forces. According to the section, what can happen to it as its temperature increases?

choices.text: It can become a gas directly, without first becoming a liquid.
It must always melt into a liquid before it can become a gas.
choices.why: Substances with very weak intermolecular forces can skip the liquid phase and become gases directly, a process called sublimation.

choices.text: Its molecules break apart into separate atoms.
choices.why: Warming overcomes the forces between molecules, not the covalent bonds inside them. The molecules separate from each other intact.

choices.text: It stays solid at every temperature, because weak forces can't be overcome.
choices.why: Weak forces are the easiest to overcome, so such a substance leaves the solid phase readily as it warms.

explanation: As the temperature increases, substances with very weak intermolecular forces become gases directly, in a process called sublimation. Substances with somewhat stronger interactions become liquids first.
